title: A page a day
hook: since 1923 people have read one page a day, finishing the Talmud in about seven and a half years

segments.voice: Yesterday Rabbi Chanina learned most of all from his students. Your line was most from students. Did someone younger teach you something? Day two hundred ninety-three.

In January 2020, a football stadium in New Jersey filled up, and it wasn't for football. Tens of thousands of people came to celebrate finishing a book. The same book, at the same pace, read by people all over the world: in Jerusalem, in Buenos Aires, on commuter trains, on phones, in the early morning before work. They'd been reading it for seven and a half years, one page a day. Today, the last day of our taste of Talmud, we meet Daf Yomi, the daily page.
screen: `A STADIUM FULL OF READERS.` → `ONE BOOK, ALL OVER THE WORLD.` → `SEVEN AND A HALF YEARS.`

segments.voice: Daf is page; we met it on day two hundred seventy, when we found there's no page one. Yomi means daily. The idea came from Rabbi Meir Shapiro of Lublin, in Poland. In 1923, at a large gathering of Jewish leaders in Vienna, he proposed that Jews everywhere learn the same page of the Babylonian Talmud on the same day. A traveler could walk into any study house in the world and join the page. People who'd never have tackled the whole Talmud could do it one page at a time. The first cycle began that fall. The Talmud has more than twenty-seven hundred double-sided pages, so a full cycle takes about seven and a half years. When a cycle ends, there's a celebration called a siyum, a finishing. That stadium in 2020 was one of them. Remember the water on Akiva's stone. A page a day is drops. Hillel, Shammai, Honi's circle, the oven that couldn't be decided, Beruriah's reading, the orchard, Yavneh, the white face, Sarah's words, the students who teach their teachers: every story we've tasted these weeks is on those pages, somewhere in the cycle. People learn Daf Yomi in many ways: in synagogues, in podcasts, in women's study groups that have held their own siyums. The point isn't to finish fast. It's to keep going, together, with people you'll never meet, on the very same page.
screen: `DAF: PAGE. YOMI: DAILY.` · `VIENNA, 1923: THE SAME PAGE.` · `SEVEN AND A HALF YEARS.` · `DROPS ON THE STONE.` · then, large: `A PAGE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back over our taste of Talmud. Settle, and breathe. Of all the stories these weeks, which one stayed with you? Hillel in the snow? The carob tree? These and these? Let one come back. Now think of a short passage you could read today, from any text you love. A paragraph, a psalm, a page. Picture reading it slowly, the way people read the daily page, and knowing others are reading too. The bell holds the time.
Daf Yomi. The daily page: one page of Talmud a day, the whole of it in about seven and a half years, together.
Your line: a page a day. Today, read one short passage slowly, and tomorrow, read the next one. Day two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Many Jews worldwide study the day's page of Talmud, alone, with a partner, in a morning class or through recorded lectures, and celebrate each completed cycle with a siyum.
